topic: Keeping domain failures HTTP-agnostic with Spring MVC exception mapping
tomorrowTopic: Testing domain-to-HTTP exception mappings with MockMvc

hook.headline: Your domain should not know HTTP
hook.hook: Annotating a domain exception with a web status is convenient, but it couples business code to one delivery protocol. Keep the failure semantic in the domain; translate it at the HTTP boundary.
hook.visualCaption: domain failure → web adapter → HTTP response

mentalModel.title: Translate at the boundary
mentalModel.coreIdea: A domain or application failure describes what went wrong in business terms. Spring MVC infrastructure can translate that failure into an HTTP status and ProblemDetail without making domain code depend on Spring Web.
mentalModel.keyOutcome: Business code remains reusable while the web layer owns HTTP-specific semantics.
mentalModel.mentalShortcut: domain names the failure; adapter chooses the protocol response

code.title: Keep Spring Web at the edge
code.intro: The exception is plain Java; the MVC advice owns the HTTP mapping.
code.highlightReason: The Spring-specific translation starts at the web boundary, not in the domain exception.
code.takeaway: Do not make domain exceptions carry HTTP concerns unless that coupling is an intentional architectural choice.
code.professionalNote: Spring MVC supports @ExceptionHandler methods in controller advice, and those methods can return ProblemDetail. The choice of 404 is your API contract; Spring does not infer domain semantics for you.

production.title: Avoid protocol leakage
production.scenario: An order service is called by REST today and later by a message consumer. Its OrderNotFound exception was originally annotated with @ResponseStatus.
problems: The domain package now depends on Spring Web semantics.
A non-HTTP caller inherits an HTTP-oriented design decision that has no meaning in its protocol.
production.professionalApproach: Keep domain/application failures expressed in business language. In the MVC adapter, map known failures to documented statuses and problem types; map failures separately in other adapters.
production.debugClue: If changing an HTTP status requires editing a domain exception, inspect whether transport concerns have leaked across the boundary.

interview.question: Should you put @ResponseStatus directly on domain exceptions?
interview.answer: Usually not when you want a clean domain/application boundary. @ResponseStatus is a Spring Web concern, so placing it on a domain exception couples that type to HTTP. A common design is to keep the exception protocol-agnostic and translate it in @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler. That also lets another adapter map the same failure differently. Direct annotation can be reasonable in a deliberately web-centric application, but it is an architectural trade-off, not a requirement.
remember: the web adapter owns HTTP status and response shape
